# SpecArch toolchain: business requirements document

Version 1.8.1 of the specification: why the system is built, for whom, and what the business asks of it, 6 stakeholders, 10 needs and 146 requirements, in the order of the business requirements specification of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148. How each requirement is designed and verified is in the requirements specification.

## 1. Purpose and scope

The `specarch` command: it validates SpecArch specifications and makes
documents and code from them. This folder is the specification, with no
language, library or build tool in it; how one stack implements it is in
`implementation/<stack>/`.

Owners: specarch-maintainers.

## 2. Problem

The specification of a system is scattered over documents that disagree with each other and drift from the code, so the people who build it guess at what was meant, a reviewer cannot see why a choice was made or what it rests on, and the people who use the system first see it at acceptance, where every change is the most expensive.

Who it hurts: specification-author, implementer, reviewer.

**Insight:** Every part of SpecArch is judged by one question, whether it makes a human decision faster, more accurate or traceable (docs/principles.md, Goal); the problem is what that question answers.

## 3. Goals

The outcomes the owner of the system wants, each with what is counted, the value today and the value wanted, and the needs that serve it.

| Goal | Statement | Measure | Baseline | Target | By | Priority | Status | Served by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GOAL-1 | Every decision in a specification can be traced back to what it rests on and forward to what it decides. | Share of accepted requirements whose needs, satisfying elements and verifying tests are all named, as the traceability matrix counts them. |   | 100 percent of accepted requirements |   | must | accepted | NEED-5, NEED-6 |
| GOAL-2 | A specification is never quietly wrong. | Defects per release whose cause is a problem in the specification that no rule of the validator reported. |   | 0 per release |   | must | accepted | NEED-1, NEED-9 |
| GOAL-3 | The documents and the code never drift from the specification. | Generated files that differ from what the specification writes, as the landing check counts them. |   | 0 at every landing |   | must | accepted | NEED-2, NEED-3 |
| GOAL-4 | The next human decision is cheap to take, early and from what is already written. | Share of open questions that gaps --next puts with who decides, what it blocks and the command that records the answer. |   | 100 percent of open questions |   | should | accepted | NEED-4, NEED-7, NEED-8, NEED-10 |

## 4. Out of scope

What the system will not do, decided on purpose, so a question or a change request that asks for it is answered here.

| Entry | Statement | Until | Rules out |
|---|---|---|---|
| OUT-1 | SpecArch does not run, host or deploy the system it specifies; it writes the documents, the code and the checks, and the project's own pipeline runs them. | not planned |   |
| OUT-2 | SpecArch does not track who does what by when; that stays in the team's tracker, and the specification holds the scope and the order only. | not planned |   |
| OUT-3 | SpecArch has no graphical editor; a specification is YAML text, reviewed in version control. | not planned |   |

**Insight on OUT-1:** Running the system would tie SpecArch to one host and one stack, against writing a design once and building it in more than one language.

**Insight on OUT-2:** The delivery changes when a person is ill or an agent finishes early while the system does not (ADR-242), so the tracker keeps what changes with it.

**Insight on OUT-3:** A text file shows every change as a diff a reviewer reads and a merge resolves, which a drawing tool's file does not.

## 5. Quality goals

The qualities that matter most, in rank order: when two pull apart, the higher rank wins.

| Rank | Quality goal | Quality | Statement | Requirements |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | QG-1 | functional-suitability | A specification the validator passes holds no problem one of its rules could have reported, and both validator builds print the same lines for it. |   |
| 2 | QG-2 | interaction-capability | Every problem names the entry, the rule and what to write, so the analyst settles it without reading SpecArch's code. |   |
| 3 | QG-3 | maintainability | A rule, a document or a generator is added in one place per build and checked by one case of its own. |   |

**Insight on QG-1:** A wrong answer from the validator is the problem itself, a specification that is quietly wrong.

## 6. Stakeholders

| Stakeholder | Who they are | Concerns |
|---|---|---|
| specification-author | A person or an assistant who writes a specification in SpecArch and keeps it current. | A mistake in a specification is caught before anyone builds on it; A large specification stays navigable |
| implementer | A developer who builds a system from a specification, in one of possibly several stacks. | The design says enough to build from, including how values travel; A change in the design is noticed in every implementation of it |
| reviewer | A person who reviews a specification or the documents made from it before work starts. | Every design element traces to a requirement, and every requirement to a test; The reasoning behind a choice is written next to it |
| operator | A person who installs, releases and runs the built system. | Release, rollback and commissioning are written down and checkable |
| ci-job | The continuous-integration job that checks every change of a project that uses SpecArch. | Every check runs with one command and answers with an exit status |
| owner | The person who owns SpecArch, decides its design where a question is put to them, and approves its releases. | A design choice put to them is explained in plain words with an example, so it can be settled in one reading; What was decided, by whom and on what date is written in the specification, not in a conversation |

## 8. Business requirements

Each requirement as the business asks it: its statement, how important it is, where it stands, the needs it refines and the goals those needs serve.

| Requirement | Statement | Priority | Status | Needs | Goals |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SA-31 | specarch generate tests shall write, through the plug-in for an implementation file's stack, one test per design test and one per worked example, in Go, in Swift with Swift Testing, or in Dart with package:test or flutter_test, setting up the fixture, making the call and checking the expected outcome through a harness the project writes, so that the generated tests are the same on every project of that language. | should | accepted | NEED-9 | GOAL-2 |
| SA-120 | specarch generate tests, given a module and the estate it belongs to, shall write one integration test per call the module makes into another module of the estate, pinning both modules by name and version, with the golden path and the red paths the called operation's contract implies, in the test language of the calling module's implementation file, the tests of the calls into one module in one file of their own. | should | proposed | NEED-9 | GOAL-2 |
| SA-29 | A specification shall be able to declare the dependencies an operation calls with a time limit per call, an idempotency key on an operation, the validity of an entity's records, how a session ends, and a guard on a data change, and specarch validate shall check each against the design and derive the red cases each implies. | must | accepted | NEED-9 | GOAL-2 |
| SA-28 | specarch derive shall write a draft test for every derived case that no test covers, and shall never overwrite a test or write one for a subject an open must or should question holds up. | should | accepted | NEED-9 | GOAL-2 |
| SA-111 | specarch derive shall draft the fixture, input and expected outcome of a derived case wherever the design fixes them, shall add them on request to a test that has none, and the test plan shall say how many tests the tests target writes with their bodies. | should | proposed | NEED-9 | GOAL-2 |
| SA-27 | A design test may carry its fixture, input and expected outcome as structured data in the design's own vocabulary, and the validator shall check that data against the design. | should | accepted | NEED-9 | GOAL-2 |

| SA-22 | specarch document shall list in the test plan, under Derived cases left out, every derived case of rank other that no test covers, with its subject and the reason it was left out, and shall show each requirement's harm in the traceability matrix once a requirement names one. | must | accepted | NEED-9, NEED-3 | GOAL-2, GOAL-3 |

**Insight on SA-31:** A test the specification implies is worth most when it runs; what differs between two projects in one language (how a caller signs in, how a record is stored, how a request is sent) is the harness, so the generated file needs nothing but it.

**Insight on SA-120:** What breaks at the system integration test of an estate is most often a call between two modules owned by different teams; the two designs already say the request, the answers, the permission and the time limit, so a test of each call needs nothing but a harness that runs the two modules (ADR-226).

**Insight on SA-29:** The red paths a specification could not express, a dependency down or slow, a retry, expired data, an expired session, two writers on one record, are the ones a tester forgets and a live system meets; once the design says them, the tests follow from it like every other case.

**Note on SA-29:** From RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, 2022, clause 9.2.2: A request method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request; PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are idempotent. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110>

**Note on SA-29:** From OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: All sessions should implement an idle timeout and an absolute timeout. <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html>

**Insight on SA-28:** The tests a specification implies are only worth listing if writing them out is cheap; a draft the author completes is cheaper than a warning the author copies.

**Insight on SA-111:** A generated test whose body is written by hand is a test nobody runs until someone writes it; most of a call is already in the design, and saying how many bodies are owed shows what is left (ADR-213).

**Insight on SA-27:** A generator can only write a test from data it can read, and data checked against the design cannot describe a record that could never exist.

**Insight on SA-21:** Every case a design implies cannot be tested on every project, so the sample is chosen by risk, and the risk is read from the specification rather than from a tester's memory.

**Note on SA-21:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 1, General concepts, 2022, clause 4.1.6: Exhaustive testing is not possible in practice, so the tests run are a sample of all the tests that could be run.

**Note on SA-21:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 1, General concepts, 2022, clause 4.2.2: Risk-based testing uses the risks of the item under test to decide what to test and how much.

**Note on SA-21:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-4, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 4, Test techniques, 2021, clause 5.4.1: Error guessing designs test cases from knowledge of the mistakes that are commonly made.

**Insight on SA-22:** A case left out is a decision, and a decision the reader cannot see is one nobody can question.

**Insight on SA-128:** The tests a specification implies are only worth what a run of them in the customer's environment shows, and that environment is run by people who have neither the specification nor the project's harness; a package that holds the cases as data, run by the program that made it, needs nothing on their host but that program, and its results come back as a file the specification's own test-run record maps case by case (ADR-233).

**Note on SA-128:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 3, Test documentation, 2021, clause 8: Actual results, test results and the test execution log are dynamic test documentation items: what was run, when, and with what outcome. <https://www.iso.org/standard/79429.html>

**Insight on SA-131:** A team that already has test scripts has the test cases a stakeholder wrote down, often with a step or a result missing; reading them into the specification, with a question for each missing part instead of a guess, puts that knowledge where the derived cases are, and the test joins the package once a person settles what is missing (ADR-235).

**Note on SA-131:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 3, Test documentation, 2021, clause 8: Actual results, test results and the test execution log are dynamic test documentation items: what was run, when, and with what outcome. <https://www.iso.org/standard/79429.html>

**Insight on SA-33:** Which fields are personal, which are encrypted and whether a delete can be undone are facts a client, a tester and an auditor need; written in the design, they are checked where a mistake would leak data, and the tests follow from them.

**Insight on SA-34:** Which fields a client may filter and sort by, how large a page or a request may be, and what a refusal looks like are part of the interface; a client that guesses them is refused, and a tester who does not know them misses the cases at their edges.

**Note on SA-34:** From RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs, 2023, clause 3: A problem details object carries a type URI that identifies the problem type, a short human-readable title, and the HTTP status code; a client branches on the type. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457>

**Insight on SA-35:** What runs at night or on a queue is the part of a system nobody watches, and the part a test plan forgets; written in the design, its tests follow from it like an operation's.

**Insight on SA-47:** An approval that lives only in an external engine's configuration, or in prose, cannot be checked against the roles and permissions of the design, and the rule most worth testing, that nobody approves their own request, is the one a hand-written test plan forgets.

**Insight on SA-36:** The server interface of a Go service is written by a standard OpenAPI generator in strict mode, so the document is where the design reaches the code; written by hand, it drifts from the design on the first change.

**Insight on SA-37:** The schema is where a design reaches the data, and four engines read one design four ways; the rows say each way once, and the migration written from them cannot drift from the design.

**Insight on SA-38:** A migration that has run on a database is history; writing the next one from the design, and refusing what could lose data unless it is asked for, is the expand and contract pattern kept honest by the tool.

**Insight on SA-39:** A service on dxlib binds its handlers to the document at start, so the document is the route table; written from the design, the route table cannot drift from it, and the list of unenforced constraints says where the service checks what the library does not.

**Insight on SA-40:** The handlers, tables and seeds of a dxlib service follow from its design and its dxlib document; written by hand they drift from both, and the constraints dxlib does not enforce are easy to miss.

**Insight on SA-41:** Every list page shows a row with names and counts joined onto it; written by hand, the join drifts from the relations it follows, and a client cannot tell from the document which fields it may filter by.

**Insight on SA-42:** Left out of the design, where a person goes after each step is decided by whoever builds the screen, so screens of one application drift apart, and no reviewer sees the flow until it runs.

**Insight on SA-43:** A screen written by hand drifts from the pages, states and messages the owner reviewed; written from them, it says what the design says, and a change to the design reaches the screen on the next run.

**Insight on SA-80:** A list on its own is a screen nobody can act from; the first things a person does with it are open a record and go back, and a design whose pages cannot be reached from each other cannot be shown at the user acceptance test.

**Insight on SA-81:** Forms are where people put data into the system, and where a mistake costs most; a design whose forms exist only on Next.js cannot be shown at the user acceptance test by a project on the plain JavaScript stack.

**Insight on SA-52:** The project that asked builds its screens on Next.js and Carbon, and a screen written by hand there drifts from the design as one in plain JavaScript does; sign-in comes first because it stands in front of every other screen.

**Insight on SA-53:** A menu entry that opens a page its reader is refused is reported as a broken feature, and a list is most of what a back-office screen is; the guard and the menu read one permission so they cannot drift apart.

**Insight on SA-54:** Forms and views are the rest of a back-office screen, and a form that checks less than the service refuses, or a different rule than it, sends the person a refusal they could have been spared; a hook keeps what the design cannot say in a file the generator never overwrites.

**Insight on SA-55:** Rows under a record, a confirmation that keeps a reason, and a request that waits for a second person are the parts of a back-office screen that decide what is written and by whom; drawn from the specification, the screen sends what the service takes and refuses what it would refuse.

**Insight on SA-56:** A route written by hand per operation, a key used with no entry in the second language, and colours typed again into a component library are the parts of a front end that drift from the specification without anyone seeing; generated from it, they follow it.

**Insight on SA-48:** Data passed around but never stored, a diagnostic, a summary or a token's claims, was written as an entity with a made-up key, so the generators gave it a table nobody uses and a reader of the specification could not tell it from a stored record.

**Insight on SA-49:** An API that names its properties in snake_case could not be specified without renaming its contract, and a document generated from the renamed specification would differ from the one every client already calls.

**Insight on SA-50:** A member's address or a list of phone numbers is a value with no identity that a record holds, and a design could only write its parts as loose fields of the entity or make it an entity with a made-up key.

**Insight on SA-62:** A system whose token's roles claim and permission tables write DESK_SUPERVISOR came out of extract permissions with no role at all, and a specification that wrote its roles in upper case would break the one naming rule every role and its generated names follow.

**Insight on SA-63:** A system checked by pattern rows names no permission anywhere, and a role with a `*` row beside a `get` row came out of a printer with two names and nothing saying one covers the other; the matrix a reviewer reads has to show what each role reaches.

**Insight on SA-65:** An estate of modules owned by different teams is specified one module at a time, and a module keeps another's customer number, picks from another's list and calls another's operations; with $ref reaching only its own specification, those links were prose, and nothing checked them when the two specifications met.

**Insight on SA-66:** An estate's consistency is checked where the estate is, in one run over every module, and the umbrella that does it lists and pins the modules rather than copying them, so each team's specification stays the one truth of its module.

**Insight on SA-67:** A note from inside the team must never reach the customer's documents, and a rule read by people does not keep it out; one key on the element and one check of what names it do.

**Insight on SA-68:** A promise in the customer's documents that another component keeps belongs in the specification, and without a form for it the validator asks for what satisfies and verifies it here, or the promise is left out and its trace is lost.

**Insight on SA-69:** A question that asks for a document is answered by sending it, not by deciding, and a list that puts it among the decisions asks the wrong thing of the wrong person; a split answer written in prose loses where the open half came from; and a list of every question in one cell cannot be read once a specification has many.

**Insight on SA-70:** Read from an estate's sources, each generated key, each index and each list route was a could question on every table or route, so most of the questions an owner read were noise; and what a reader read but no generator wrote back would be lost the first time the schema or the API was generated.

**Insight on SA-75:** A service that forwards by the token's audience had no place in its own specification, so the one behaviour it exists for was recorded as a surface not read; written as an element, its token, its table and its refusals are checked, drawn and tested like an operation's.

**Insight on SA-77:** A service whose operations travel in an encrypted envelope, or that streams large files, could not say so in its specification, so a client built from it would send plain JSON to an endpoint that expects an envelope, and a document would show a field table where a stream of bytes travels.

**Insight on SA-78:** The iPhone is the platform the owner's own apps are built for, and a screen written by hand there drifts from the design as one on the web does; the roadmap names SwiftUI the default for the iPhone, and the same pages drawn twice from one specification are the check that the design, not a stack, holds the screens.

**Insight on SA-82:** A member sees only their own loans, and a tenant's staff only their organisation's records, and the meta-model could say neither, so the rule lived in prose beside the role and the service enforced what no test derived and no policy carried.

**Insight on SA-83:** An identity service served routes open only to named machine clients, routes that also required a signed request, and a route closed to everyone, and each had to be written as a permission with prose, which lost the default-deny caller list and the signature, and a closed route needed a placeholder role, since a permission no role grants is a fail-closed error.

**Insight on SA-84:** An identity service issues access, refresh, step-up, delegated and machine tokens, each with its own claims and lifetime, and the claims were only in prose, so a requirement such as the actor claim never equals the subject could not be checked against the binding, a token minted for one service could be replayed at the next, and a refusal left no event behind.

**Insight on SA-88:** The clients, the roles and the trust domain are facts of the whole estate, not of one service, and every hop of a call must check the same names; kept in each module they drift apart, and kept in the umbrella they would put design into a file that only lists and pins the modules (ADR-107).

**Insight on SA-89:** An estate written from its code has its application, caller and audience checks in middleware the project writes its own way; read as nothing, the operations look open to any caller, and guessed, a condition on a grant could be written where none holds (ADR-106, ADR-109, ADR-111).

**Insight on SA-91:** In a multi-tenant suite every role's rule over every tenant-owned entity is the same expression, written by hand hundreds of times, and an entity whose rules are forgotten is reached whole by every tenant with no word from the validator (ADR-179).

**Insight on SA-92:** A website is mostly pages of copy, images and links; without a page kind for them the site is written by hand around the generated forms, and its copy has no place among the strings a translation covers (ADR-181).

**Insight on SA-93:** An information system with single sign-on had no element for the redirect, the callback, the state, the nonce and the identity token's checks, so the flow and its refusals were written by hand, untraced and untested by anything the specification produced (ADR-182).

**Insight on SA-94:** An editor or a live view is built by hand, and without a page kind for it the screen had no route, guard, menu entry, flow or derived test in the design (ADR-183).

**Problem on SA-98:** warning: requirement_unverified: no test, commissioning check or monitor verifies requirement SA-98; add verifies: [SA-98] to the test that shows it is met [requirement_unverified@requirements/requirements/design-keywords.yaml#/requirements/SA-98]

**Insight on SA-98:** State diagrams and state variables are among the most important parts of a system architecture, and the design could say only an entity's control state and its moves, so retry counts, deadlines, conditions, a second machine of an entity and the machines of things not stored were written outside the specification, undrawn and unchecked (ADR-189 to ADR-192); nothing in a machine is left to the implementation or to a reading, the owner's word of 2026-10-26 (ADR-193).

**Insight on SA-99:** A date-time without its zone is read in whatever zone the reader runs in, so the same value means two instants on two hosts and a date is turned into an instant by a guess; the owner's rule of 2026-10-26 is that a date-time carries its zone everywhere, that a zoneless one says why, and that a date meets the clock only in the zone the specification declares (ADR-193, ADR-194).

**Insight on SA-102:** A person meets an application through its pages, in the order they reach them, and the analyst writing the specification asks what each role sees first, what every person has whatever their role, and which fields a role may change or see; until each is written, the screens fall back on a menu nobody chose and a form that shows every field to everyone. A gap in the navigation is found by a check rather than by a reader, and is a question the walkthrough asks (ADR-197).

**Insight on SA-103:** The workflows read since the sequential subset was taken route a request by its amount or kind, ask a clerk to check something before anyone approves, wait for a payment to arrive, and undo a reservation when a later step fails; written outside the workflow, none of them is checked against the subject, the roles or the operations, and none gets a test.

**Insight on SA-130:** A business process changes over weeks or months, and during that time the team builds the new process while people still work by the old one; written only as the new one, what the move adds, changes and removes is found by reading two versions side by side, and the pages, approvers and tests the move reaches are found late, in acceptance.

**Insight on SA-104:** A business states many rules as cases, and keeps them as a table; written as a formula the cases nobody decided are hidden, since the formula gives a value for them anyway. A table checked for overlap and gaps names those cases, so each is decided by a person, and each rule stays a test (ADR-199).

**Insight on SA-105:** An integration is where a system most often fails in production, and the decisions that make it fail are taken in nobody's specification today; how the other system is called, what is sent, what is tried again and what the caller is answered when it fails. Written beside the call they are checked against both sides and each gets a test (ADR-200).

**Insight on SA-106:** A person checks a mapping faster on a case they recognise than on its expressions, and a mapping's decision taken on an example is checked forever after once the example is a test (ADR-207).

**Insight on SA-109:** A daemon, a scheduled loop or a system service had to be written as a job with commands, which demanded a permission and caller cases it cannot have, while its restart, crash loop, signals and bad configuration, what goes wrong with such a program, had no key and no test (ADR-211).

**Insight on SA-114:** A service that serves a browser application answers its document, its files and a health probe by hand, outside the permission and test checks, because none is an operation; a route holds what the design fixes about each, and the stack writes what only it has (ADR-216).

**Insight on SA-115:** A project that avoids a JavaScript build chain wrote its pages and the data files that mirror the specification's menus, pages and operations by hand, so every change was made twice, and no generator wrote for that stack (ADR-218).

**Insight on SA-134:** Teams that deliver to Indonesian customers hand them documents in Indonesian, and translating a generated document by hand loses the next regeneration; the catalog makes the translation part of the program.

**Insight on SA-146:** A weakness written into the design is built into every stack the design is generated for, and costs least to change while it is still a line of the specification; a warning at that line, naming what to change, makes the security decision visible to the person who writes it and to the reviewer (ADR-247).

**Note on SA-146:** From OWASP API Security Top 10, 2023, clause API1:2023: Broken object level authorisation is the most common and most damaging API weakness: an endpoint that takes an object's identifier must check that the caller may act on that object. <https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/>

**Insight on SA-147:** SARIF readers group results by a rule's tags, and a tool that traces a finding from the specification into the code needs a name it can cite across releases (ADR-247, ADR-156).

**Insight on SA-26:** Reviewers and operators read what changed and why in documents; kept apart from the specification, the history stays out of it and still reaches them.

**Note on SA-14:** From Protocol buffers compiler plug-in protocol, plugin.proto, 2024: A plug-in reads a CodeGeneratorRequest from standard input and writes a CodeGeneratorResponse to standard output; protoc writes the files, so a plug-in never touches the disk. <https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.proto>

**Insight on SA-15:** A reader can skip every Insight and Note and still read the document, or read only them to follow the reasoning; a label on each makes both possible.

**Note on SA-16:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 3, Test documentation, 2021, clause 7.2 and 8.3: A test plan and test case specifications are the test documentation items of a project. <https://www.iso.org/standard/79429.html>

**Insight on SA-46:** A system read from its sources often holds parts another team builds and changes, such as a shared table or a service behind the same gateway; the specification must describe them, since the project's code depends on them and its sources cite them, but a project that generated them would overwrite the other team's work or fight it on every change.

**Insight on SA-58:** A workflow is reviewed by people who read BPMN diagrams and run BPMN engines, so the design must reach them in that format; written by hand, the diagram drifts from the workflow on the first change, and one that cannot be read back cannot take a change made in a modeller back into the specification.

**Insight on SA-59:** The people who answer the questions judge a result faster from the code and screens than from documents, and a compiler that stops at the first gap hides every other one; a draft that says what it is, with each gap at its entry, shows both without letting unapproved code pass for approved.

**Insight on SA-60:** Reviewers and testers read a specification long before it is finished and seldom read YAML; one page they can open anywhere, search, and link into by an element's id lets them name exactly what a remark is about, which is what takes it back into the specification.

**Insight on SA-61:** Most screens of a project that comes to SpecArch were built by hand; before the generated ones replace them, the owner needs to see, page by page, where the specification and the built screen disagree, without the noise of formatting.

**Insight on SA-71:** A project on sqlc writes its queries by hand, and most of them are the same few shapes of every entity; writing those from the design keeps them in step with the tables, and a comparison with the file written by hand shows where the two disagree before the generated one replaces it.

**Insight on SA-87:** A data change typed by hand against a live system is where a wrong condition changes a thousand records instead of one; a script written from the guard checks the state it expects, shows the change before making it and counts what it changed, so the mistake is refused rather than committed.

**Insight on SA-90:** The people who use a system and the people who run it read a manual and an operations guide, not a technical specification; written by hand both drift from the pages and the procedures, and written from the specification they show early what a page asks of a person, which is where a change request starts.

**Note on SA-90:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4.12: The operation process uses the system in its intended environment and supports its users. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

**Insight on SA-116:** A project writes the fake records its developers work against by hand, in SQL, and they drift from the specification at every change of a field, an enum or a relation; drawing them from the entities with a fixed seed keeps them in step and byte-identical, so generate --check reads a stale seed as it reads a stale migration.

**Insight on SA-121:** A compose file, a set of manifests or a host image written by hand repeats what the implementation file's deployment already says and drifts from it at the next setting or port; a full regression run on an environment an earlier test left behind passes or fails on what that test wrote; and the quickest way to run a thing by hand is to write its password next to it, so the generated files leave every secret to the host (ADR-227).

**Insight on SA-148:** A business requirements document, a requirements specification, a technical specification and a test document are what a customer signs and files, as PDF; written from the specification they cannot drift from it, and a book written from an incomplete specification shows its gaps where they are instead of hiding them (ADR-248).

**Note on SA-148:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 9.3: The business requirements specification describes the organisation's motivation for the system: its purpose, scope, stakeholders, goals and the business requirements, before the system requirements. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Note on SA-148:** From ISO 32000-2, Document management, Portable document format, Part 2, PDF 2.0, 2020, clause 14.8: A tagged PDF carries a logical structure of standard types, headings, paragraphs, lists, tables and links, beside the page content, so the text can be extracted, reflowed and read by assistive technology; content not part of the document, such as running headers and page numbers, is marked as an artifact. <https://www.iso.org/standard/75839.html>

**Insight on SA-149:** The formal documents go to readers who work in different tools - Markdown in the repository, Word for review and sign-off, PDF for distribution - and each form written from the one Markdown keeps them from saying different things (ADR-249).

**Note on SA-149:** From ISO/IEC 29500-1, Office Open XML File Formats, Fundamentals and Markup Language Reference, 2016, clause 11.3: A WordprocessingML package holds the main document part and the parts it is related to, such as the styles, the numbering definitions, the headers and the footers, each reached through a relationship of its own type. <https://www.iso.org/standard/71691.html>

**Insight on SA-32:** How a decimal, a text column or a missing value is held on a stack is decided once and read by every generator and every agent; without the table each implementation file restates it in prose, each a little differently.

**Insight on SA-135:** A product requirements document is written beside a full specification only for what the specification has no home for, the problem, the measured goals, the boundary and the order of qualities (ADR-242); giving them keys in the requirements stage makes one source instead of two that drift.

**Note on SA-135:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 9.3: The business requirements specification states the business purpose, the scope, the goals and the problem the system addresses, before the stakeholder and system requirements. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Note on SA-135:** From arc42, the template for architecture documentation, 8.2, clause 1: Introduction and goals: the requirements overview, the three to five most important quality goals in order, and the stakeholders, read first because the architecture is judged against them. <https://arc42.org/overview>

**Insight on SA-136:** Every later answer rests on the problem and the measured goals, so their absence is shown first; a compiler for specifications never refuses to read a specification for missing intent, so each is a warning, and on a small tool's lean specification a warning that shows on every run teaches people to skip warnings, so there it is a question (the owner's decision 3 of ADR-242).

**Insight on SA-137:** The intent is the first thing a reviewer and an agent read, so it is one page of its own, and it is the chapter arc42 opens with; a goal column shows which goal a requirement serves without a second document.

**Insight on SA-138:** Every other answer rests on the problem and the goals; a missing problem is a gap and not a refusal, so it never changes whether gaps fails a run.

**Insight on SA-139:** The owner chose flags with prompts on a terminal (2026-11-05), so scripts and agents keep working unchanged and a person at the terminal is asked in plain words.

**Insight on SA-11:** One file for a whole system grows past what a reader can navigate; a tree whose folder names say what is inside lets the reader walk to a thing.

**Note on SA-12:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4: The technical processes run from business or mission analysis and stakeholder needs definition (6.4.2) through requirements definition (6.4.3), design (6.4.4 and 6.4.5), implementation (6.4.7), verification (6.4.9), transition (6.4.10) and validation (6.4.11). <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

**Note on SA-12:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.3 and 6.4: Stakeholder needs are defined first and then transformed into system requirements; each requirement carries attributes and traces to its source. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-23:** A change, a defect or a release happens once and moves through statuses; kept in the specification it would turn it into a change log, and kept nowhere it could not be checked against what the specification says.

**Note on SA-23:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.3.5 and 6.4.13: Configuration management records and controls changes to the system and its baselines; maintenance handles the problems and modification requests raised after transition. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

**Insight on SA-24:** A version number is a promise to everyone who depends on the system; one that steps less than its contents say breaks a client that trusted it.

**Note on SA-24:** From Semantic Versioning, 2.0.0, clause rules 4, 6 to 9 and 11: A major version zero is for initial development; patch, minor and major versions step for fixes, additions and incompatible changes; a pre-release version is marked with a hyphen; precedence compares major, minor and patch numerically, and a pre-release ranks below its normal version. <https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html>

**Insight on SA-25:** A release record says what a release carries; only a comparison of the two versions shows whether the specification changed that way.

**Note on SA-13:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 5.2.8: Rationale and source are attributes every requirement should carry. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-73:** Regulated customers take the source into a repository of their own and build and run production themselves; a deployment guide written for the vendor's hosts says nothing to them, and a handover written by hand drifts from the specification.

**Note on SA-73:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.4.10: The transition process establishes the capability to provide the service in its operational environment. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

**Insight on SA-96:** The installed program is often all a person, a CI job or an agent has; a description built from the same definitions as the program cannot name a flag it lacks, a JSON form lets a program drive it without parsing text, and a dry run shows each file before any is written.

**Insight on SA-119:** The facts a person or an agent needs to pick a feature are spread over the agent guide, the capabilities listing, the help topics, the manual and the design documents, each organised by command; a person in a situation does not know which command to look up, and a guide that is not checked against the program names features it no longer has within a release or two.

**Insight on SA-112:** An agent uses a tool it is handed and a skill it has loaded far more readily than a command a repository tells it about; made from the same definitions as help and capabilities, neither can name an input the program does not take (ADR-214).

**Insight on SA-101:** A proposal that is not yet part of the specification is lost when it is only said, and once it is in the text nobody can tell what was proposed, by which way it came in, and what was turned down and why; kept as a record it is checked like the other records, the person's decision on it is written down, and the decision it became can be traced back to it (ADR-196).

**Insight on SA-117:** Real requirements come from conversations, meetings, chats and emails that leave no record of who said what and when; kept as records beside the specification, checked like the others and cited by the decisions they led to, a stakeholder's words are traceable, a changed attachment shows, and a role nobody heard shows before it objects at acceptance (ADR-220).

**Note on SA-117:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.4.3: Each requirement is traceable to its source: the stakeholder need or the document it comes from. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-132:** A team that delivers from a specification is asked how big it is, what is still open and with whom, and how far it has come; answered from what the specification and its records hold, the answer is the same for everyone who asks, and an effort nobody recorded shows as missing instead of being guessed (ADR-237).

**Insight on SA-125:** Whether the tests passed is known only to the build that ran them, in a results file a CI job throws away; kept as a record with each result tied to the test and so to the elements and requirements it verifies, the question of which requirement was shown met on which build and which element keeps failing is answered from the records, and a testcase the specification does not know shows instead of being lost (ADR-230).

**Note on SA-125:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3, Software and systems engineering, Software testing, Part 3, Test documentation, 2021, clause 8: Actual results, test results and the test execution log are dynamic test documentation items: what was run, when, and with what outcome. <https://www.iso.org/standard/79429.html>

**Insight on SA-127:** Choosing between two implementations of one design is a decision taken from CI logs, scan reports and what people remember of the build; one table built from the kept inputs, every missing result marked rather than left blank and the comparison cited by the decision as a source, makes the choice quick to take and to review and keeps it traceable to its evidence (ADR-232).

**Insight on SA-17:** A placeholder looks like data and every tool downstream treats it as data; a question says in the specification itself that something is not known, so nothing can be built on it unseen.

**Note on SA-17:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 5.2.6: A complete set of requirements holds no to-be-defined, to-be-specified or to-be-resolved clause; resolving them is iterative, within a time set by risk and dependency. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Note on SA-17:** From IEEE Std 830-1998, IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, 1998, clause 4.3.3: A to-be-determined item is accompanied by why it is open, what must be done to close it, who is responsible and by when.

**Insight on SA-107:** The questions gaps lists are answered by people, who answer better one question at a time with a choice and a recommended answer than a list at once; ranking by what an answer unblocks puts first the question whose answer moves the most work.

**Insight on SA-108:** A first draft of a small tool met a wall of errors before anything could be shown, most of them tests the program can write itself; the lean profile lets such a draft validate, keeps every demand visible as a warning, and is tightened by one word, while the smallest specification and its next step take the guessing out of the first minutes.

**Note on SA-20:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.3.3.6: Requirements validation is subject to approval by the project authority and the key stakeholders. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-30:** The owner of an existing system reads a partial specification to find out what the documents and the code really say and where they part; a section of either that produced nothing is the first thing to look at, and it cannot be seen without the outline.

**Insight on SA-44:** Reading a large system by hand misses the element nobody happened to look at, and a citation without the commit it was read at goes stale while still looking precise; extraction is rerun to see what changed, so any difference that is not a change in the sources hides the one that is.

**Insight on SA-45:** The comparison between surfaces, and between the documents and the code, is where a specification extracted from an existing system finds what is wrong with it; done by hand it is skipped where the two look alike, and a choice made quietly between two sources hides the disagreement the owner must settle.

**Insight on SA-57:** People never write a complete specification, and the people who will use a system see it first at the user acceptance test; a remark that cannot name the element it is about, or that has no way back into the specification, is lost or applied by hand where the next generation overwrites it.

**Insight on SA-64:** A document in another language gave its outline and nothing else, every table a could line, since the commitment words, the headers and the units were English in the code; a wrong or missing word has to be one line in a data file that the project changes without a release.

**Insight on SA-110:** Most requirement documents are PDF or Word, and a records repository also holds decks, registers and correspondence; converting each to Markdown by hand is a step nobody reviews, and the converters drop Word's computed clause numbers, so the citation would no longer name the clause a reader of the file finds (ADR-212).

**Insight on SA-113:** Registers and spreadsheets are the data model of many real systems, kept in a records repository beside the controlled documents, and a reader that typed a column by its first value or dropped a column two files disagree on would write a guess into the design (ADR-215).

**Insight on SA-72:** A specification nobody compares with its code drifts and is then read by nobody; a gate that fails on every old difference is switched off, and one whose allowlist may grow lets the drift back in.

**Insight on SA-76:** The table a gateway forwards by was readable by nothing, and a gateway no check compares with its table drifts as every other part of a specification nobody compares with its code does.

**Insight on SA-79:** A route registered through the module's own constants was a question where the code was plain, and a handler that takes every unmatched request was dropped with no question, which is the one thing a reader may never do.

**Insight on SA-85:** Writing the decision and removing the question by hand is two edits in two files under a number that must be the next one, which an agent got wrong often enough; and a dispatcher that must parse the question out of a message, or open the specification to find its folder, is one that reads the text instead.

**Note on SA-85:** From IEEE Std 830-1998, IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, 1998, clause 4.3.3: A to-be-determined item is accompanied by why it is open, what must be done to close it, who is responsible and by when.

**Insight on SA-86:** Before approving, the reviewer wants to see what the refinement changed against what the old documents said, and whether anything of them was left behind; read by hand from the citations that is slow and skipped where the two look alike.

**Note on SA-86:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.3.3.6: Requirements validation is subject to approval by the project authority and the key stakeholders. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-97:** A specification is layered decisions, and a reader who changes one wants to know what it rests on and what rests on it before the change; written as links the toolchain checks, the chain is read in one command rather than reconstructed from the records, which is the goal of docs/principles.md.

**Note on SA-97:** From Documenting architecture decisions, 2011: A decision record is never edited once accepted; a later decision supersedes it, and the record says which. <https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions>

**Insight on SA-118:** What a stakeholder said reaches the analyst in a chat or a call, and the agent that writes it down must not fill in who, when or what was answered, since a guessed fact reads as a fact; taking every field as an option and sending back the questions to ask keeps the record true to what the analyst reported, and the decision that follows cites the record rather than a source declared for every chat message (ADR-220).

**Note on SA-118:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.4.3: Each requirement is traceable to its source: the stakeholder need or the document it comes from. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-129:** A stakeholder nobody listed is the one who objects first at acceptance, and the list is confirmed by a person, not by a rule; a warning that stands in every output until a role confirms it keeps the gap visible without stopping the work, which a compiler for specifications never does.

**Note on SA-129:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 5.2.2: The stakeholders of the system are identified, so that every class of stakeholder with a legitimate interest in the system is represented. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-133:** An approval says a role read the documents; a role nobody ever heard approving is the one most likely to object first at acceptance, and an approval that names where the documents were read can be traced back to the session and the people in it.

**Note on SA-133:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.3.3.6: Requirements validation is subject to approval by the project authority and the key stakeholders. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

**Insight on SA-1:** The schema is the one definition of a file's shape; checking it first means every later rule can assume the shape.

**Note on SA-6:** From The go command, Go documentation, 1.26: The Go tools print one problem per line as file:line, which editors and CI already parse. <https://go.dev/doc/>

**Insight on SA-51:** People fix a specification the way they fix code, from a compiler's list of problems, one place at a time; a tool that refuses an invalid specification, or lists errors and questions in different places, hides what the author has to fix.

**Note on SA-51:** From Static Analysis Results Interchange Format (SARIF) Version 2.1.0, 2020, clause result: A result names its rule, its kind and level, its locations, and partial fingerprints that recognise it in a later run. <https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html>

**Insight on SA-74:** An editor or any other program that draws from a specification would otherwise load the files itself, a second loader in another language that drifts from the first; one command in both builds, printing one byte form, gives it what specarch reads and lets the conformance suite hold the two builds to the same document.

**Insight on SA-95:** A file's version line is its promise of which rules it is written against (ADR-055); reading every version side by side keeps every specification that exists valid while the format moves on, and an author learns from one warning what moves the file and with which command (ADR-186).

**Insight on SA-100:** A reader decides on a rule faster and more accurately from its result on a case they recognise than from its formula; validate says only that an example does not hold, so the result of a passing example, the steps that gave a wrong one and the effect of a proposed formula on the examples were worked out by hand, which is the cost the goal names (ADR-195).

**Insight on SA-126:** A broker, a framework or a protocol that nothing in the design needs is the technology choice that costs a delivery most, and the one a reviewer sees last, when it is already built; a warning at the binding makes the decision to adopt it visible where it is written, and names what would make it traceable to a requirement, a rejected simpler option or the organisation's baseline (ADR-231).

**Insight on SA-140:** A work package describes the delivery, not the system, so it is a record beside the release records; naming requirements only keeps one way to say which design elements and tests it covers, the satisfy and verify links (ADR-242, ADR-245).

**Note on SA-140:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.3.1: The project planning process defines the work of the project and divides it into packages of activities and tasks that can be estimated, scheduled and assigned. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

**Insight on SA-141:** Ready is QA's entry criterion and done its exit criterion, so both are checked, not just written; the order, overlap, release and configuration checks show a plan that cannot be followed before anyone starts on it, and each is a warning because a plan is never refused (ADR-242, ADR-245).

**Insight on SA-142:** The project manager reads per package what is done, in progress or blocked and by what, and QA tests each package as it lands; a specification without work packages keeps the documents it had (ADR-242, ADR-245).

**Insight on SA-143:** A project manager starts from the requirements and the design, not from an empty tracker, and the order is already in the reference graph the diagrams draw; proposing from it and checking readiness with the validator's own rules answers who takes what next, and whether they can start now (ADR-242, ADR-246).

**Note on SA-143:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, Systems and software engineering, Software life cycle processes, 2017, clause 6.3.1: The project planning process defines the work of the project and divides it into packages of activities and tasks that can be estimated, scheduled and assigned. <https://www.iso.org/standard/63712.html>

**Insight on SA-144:** Whoever takes a package should not have to walk the satisfy, verify and needs links by hand, and the same page serves a person and an agent; DevOps sees what a package changes in operation before it lands (ADR-242, ADR-246).

**Insight on SA-145:** The project manager keeps the tracker they already use; each side wins on its own fields and a change on the wrong side is said, never taken silently, so the plan does not drift (ADR-242, ADR-246).

**Note on SA-145:** From RFC 4180, Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files, 2005: Fields containing line breaks (CRLF), double quotes, and commas should be enclosed in double-quotes. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4180>

## 9. Constraints

| Constraint | Kind | Statement |
|---|---|---|
| CON-1 | technical | Every keyword that a standard already has is taken from that standard with its meaning; SpecArch adds a keyword only where none exists. |
| CON-2 | technical | The program installs with one command and runs in CI without a network. |
| CON-3 | legal | Every dependency is open source under an OSI-approved licence, pinned, and scanned before it is taken. |
| CON-4 | organisational | The repository is public and holds generic material only; no employer's, client's or product's data enters it. |

**Insight on CON-1:** A reader who knows JSON Schema, OpenAPI or AsyncAPI should not learn a second name for the same thing.

**Note on CON-1:** From JSON Schema, a media type for describing JSON documents, 2020-12: Field keywords such as type, properties, required, enum, format and the limits. <https://json-schema.org/specification>

**Note on CON-1:** From OpenAPI Specification, 3.1.0: Endpoint keywords such as paths, parameters, requestBody and responses. <https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0>

## 10. Assumptions

| Assumption | Statement |
|---|---|
| ASSUME-1 | A specification is kept in version control, so its history lives there and in history files, never inside the specification. |
| ASSUME-2 | The people and assistants who write specifications can read YAML and a C-like expression. |

**Insight on ASSUME-1:** Without this the files would need change logs, which the Low IQ Tax principle forbids.

## 11. Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| specification | One folder tree rooted at specarch.yaml that describes one system through its life cycle. Its design side, everything but implementation/, is the SpecArch Definition (SDF). |
| implementation file | A file named <name>.<stack>.specarch-implementation.yaml (SIF) that says how one stack builds the specification. |
| stage | One of the six life-cycle parts a specification may keep, each in a folder of its name; requirements, design, implementation, tests, deployment, commissioning. |
| section | One top-level key of the merged specification, such as entities or checks; each belongs to one stage. |
| diagnostic | One problem in one file, printed as one line with the file, the line, the severity, the YAML path, the rule and a sentence. |
| rule | The name of one check the validator makes, as the Rule enum lists them. |
| target | What a document or code command produces, such as techspec or openapi, written into the folder the implementation file names for it. |
| plug-in | An executable named specarch-gen-<target> on PATH that produces a code target specarch does not build in. |
| golden scenario | A test of the path that succeeds. |
| red scenario | A test of a path that is refused. |
